CVE-2026-123633 (HTTP/2) and CVE-2026-121810 (HTTP/3) are use-after-free bugs in connection draining with proxying to a backend. CVE-2026-123634 is a resolver use-after-free needing a request-derived proxy_pass target plus SSI or mirror subrequests. CVE-2026-113425 hits the mail proxy when proxy and auth_http are combined.

- Root chain: code execution lands as the NGINX worker, then a separate Linux kernel SCTP use-after-free or double free (code introduced in Linux 4.15) escalates to root. The researchers say the chain also crossed a Docker container boundary. That kernel bug has no CVE and no fix yet. ATT&CK per the report: T1190, T1068, T1611.

- Exploit reality: the public PoC for CVE-2026-123007 (GitHub, November 18) gets code execution against NGINX 1.31.8 with HTTP/2 over TLS in a Docker lab. It needs x86-64 with AVX-512 and a particular glibc memory-copy routine, has to defeat ASLR, and pushes roughly 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic down a single connection. A proxy terminating HTTP/2 in front of NGINX will most likely stop it. The discoverers and another team hold working exploits but withheld the final steps. Fake exploit repos are circulating, so vet anything you pull.

The warning signs come from CIRCL's advisory; the grep is from the report's checks.

Run nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -nE 'http2|http3|quic|resolver|proxy_pass|mirror|ssi on|auth_http' to see which flaws apply. Check bundled NGINX in container images, appliances and load balancers. Community ingress-nginx is retired with no fix planned. After upgrading, do a full restart, because a reload keeps the old binary running.

If patching waits, disable the feature behind each flaw. Turning off HTTP/2 covers only CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, and disabling mirror alone leaves CVE-2026-123634 open. On hosts that do not need SCTP, add install sctp /bin/false under /etc/modprobe.d/ and confirm with lsmod, since an already-loaded module stays active until reboot or removal. Check sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space (2 is full) and look for services launched with setarch -R. Preserve error logs and worker core dumps before restarting.

Researchers observed that low-privilege database accounts — granted only temporary table rights — can trigger memory-corruption bugs in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and ClickHouse engine code to achieve full OS-level RCE. The Oracle chain (CVE-2026-114819, CVSS 9.9) requires no credentials at all. SQL permission boundaries do not constrain memory-unsafe execution paths — the blast radius begins at the database tier and extends outward from there. Runtime segmentation restricting east-west traffic from database hosts helps contain post-compromise lateral movement before it reaches adjacent services.

#CloudSecurity #ZeroTrust

🔗 Full TRC analysis: https://t.co/nTx00Kc0xI

A database user with almost no permissions can potentially turn a SQL connection into a shell on the server

Security researcher Zheng Yu demonstrated this against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, and found a separate attack chain against Oracle

The research exposes a gap between database permissions and the code those permissions allow users to reach

Even when an account cannot access application tables, it can still interact with components such as query optimizers, aggregate functions and binary data parsers

A memory corruption flaw in one of those components can turn limited SQL access into operating-system command execution

The demonstrations included:

PostgreSQL — CVE-2026-116331

A type-confusion bug in the query planner allows a default login role to construct objects in its temporary schema and eventually execute commands as the PostgreSQL service account

MySQL — CVE-2026-101786

An out-of-bounds write in windowed BIT_OR aggregation can be triggered using prepared statements and oversized binary input

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events

In the first implementation of the translation table events, it was only
possible to announce:

* ADD: new locally detected client
* DEL: disappeared local client

If an ADD event was queued and then a DEL event was queued in the same
timeslot, it is valid to destroy both events because nothing actually
changed for remode nodes

But with commit 3c4f7ab60cc2 ("batman-adv: improve the TT component to
support runtime flag changes") and subsequent changes, it could also happen
that there are extra ADD events:

* ADD: NEW locally detected client
* ADD: already existing client with new flags
* DEL: disappeared local client

The first and the last type of event could in theory still be removed
together from the (to be announced) events queue. But if the "update flags"
ADD is dropped together with the DEL, it would still leave global
translation table of a remote node in the incorrect state - believing that
the client didn't disappear.

If a detected client was previously announced, a DEL event must only
overwrite the "update flags" ADD but the DEL itself must still continue to
exist in the (to be anounced) events queue. For now, adjustment of the
announced flags is used for everything instead of dropping already queued
up events completely.

Similarly, a DEL followed by an ADD caused both entries to be deleted. But
the new ADD could announce flags changes which were not yet present for the
client before it was marked for DELetion. The new ADD must therefore only
overwrite the DEL - but still be kept.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: don't let the extent type hide an exhausted free-space table extent

udf table new block() takes the first block of the free-space table
extent closest to the goal. It keeps that extent's type and length
together in goal elen, subtracts one block, and deletes the extent only
if goal elen then reaches zero. UDF 2.60 section 2.3.7.1 requires the
free-space extents of an Unallocated Space Entry to be of type 1
(allocated but not recorded), and mkudffs writes them that way. For
such an extent the type bits keep goal elen non-zero, so taking its last
block leaves a type-1 extent of length zero behind, starting at the
block after the extent, which is in use.

The next allocation that picks this empty extent returns that in-use
block. Subtracting a block from 0x40000000 then borrows from the type
bits, and the extent becomes type 0 with a length of 2^30 - blocksize:
about a gigabyte of "free" space overlapping live metadata, the other
table extents and whatever lies behind the partition. From then on
blocks are handed out twice, or past the end of the partition.

Extents that udf table free blocks() adds are type 0, where the check
works, so only tables written by mkudffs or by another implementation
are affected. Nothing more than filling such a filesystem is needed:
on a fresh 1 MiB "mkudffs --space=unalloctable" image, creating empty
files until the partition is full writes file entries over the reserve
volume descriptor sequence and the backup anchor, and df then reports a
negative amount of used space.

On syzbot's images the same double allocation is what the two reports
below trip over. In the first, ftruncate() extends a new file with
enough hole extents to need a chain of allocation extent descriptors;
one AED is placed on another inode's file entry, and a later one is
placed on the block of the AED currently being filled, which
udf setup indirect aext() zeroes, so  udf add aext() finds
lengthAllocDescs out of step with its cursor. In the second, an AED
is placed past the end of the device, sb getblk() fails, and the error
path of udf do extend file() calls udf truncate extents() on an extent
list that no longer covers i size.

Keep the type separately from the length, as udf table prealloc blocks()
already does.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes

On AMD CPUs with INVLPGB, two live processes can get the same MAX ASID AVAILABLE
global ASID value. The two then hit each other's TLB entries, so each can read
or corrupt the other's memory.

The global ASID space is managed lazily. When a global ASID is freed, its bit is
set in the global asid freed bitmap. Once the free ASID search reaches the end
of the global asid used bitmap, a global flush is done to really reclaim the
lazily freed global ASIDs.

However, the current code can assign the same global ASID to two different
processes, if one process is assigned MAX ASID AVAILABLE - 1, another process
MAX ASID AVAILABLE, and both stick around (keeping their global ASID numbers in
use) until the search wraps around again. At that point a third process could
also get assigned MAX ASID AVAILABLE.

  the highest ASID stays in use, so it is not handed out again
   last global asid stays below it, so no reset
    the clear bits run out
     find next zero bit() returns MAX ASID AVAILABLE
      global asid available > 0, so the failure is not caught
       MAX ASID AVAILABLE is handed out as an ASID

A search only looks at the bits below MAX ASID AVAILABLE, so it cannot see that
this value is in use. The next failed search hands it out again, even if the
first process still holds it.

The fix used here is to reset the global ASID space after a failed search, and
to search again. If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out.

The test for !global asid available is removed, because use global asid() only
calls allocate global asid() if global asid available > 0. The remaining test is
for a condition that should be impossible.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: fix preallocation discarding before an empty allocation extent

udf discard prealloc() finds the last extent of a file by peeking at
the next one with udf next aext() and stopping when that returns 0.
The peek reads into eloc and elen, and the code then uses them as the
last extent. But when udf next aext() returns 0 they hold no defined
value: if the extent list ends in a continuation descriptor that leads
to an empty allocation extent, they describe that continuation, i.e.
the block of the empty allocation extent, one block long.

The kernel creates such lists itself: when udf delete aext() removes
the only descriptor of the last allocation extent in a list, it leaves
that allocation extent empty and the continuation to it in place.

If the last extent is a preallocation, udf discard prealloc() deletes
it with udf delete aext(), which finds the following allocation extent
empty, so it also removes the continuation and frees that allocation
extent's block. udf discard prealloc() then frees eloc and elen: that
block a second time, instead of the preallocated blocks. On a space
bitmap the preallocated blocks leak and the free block count drifts.
On an unallocated space table the second free adds a second free
extent for the same block, which is later handed out twice: fsx as run
by generic/091 and generic/263 ends up with two parts of its test file
in one block and reads back bad data.

Peek into separate variables, so that eloc and elen keep the last
extent that udf next aext() returned with 1.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners

mptcp pm nl create listen socket() starts the TCP listener directly
instead of going through mptcp listen(). It consequently misses setting
SOCK RCU FREE on the parent MPTCP socket.

tcp child process() can invoke the listener's subflow data ready()
callback without holding the MPTCP parent lock or a reference to the
parent. An authenticated MP JOIN racing with endpoint teardown can
therefore access the parent after its last reference has been dropped.
The ADD ADDR error path can also close an already published listener.

Set SOCK RCU FREE before  inet listen sk() publishes the TCP listener,
matching mptcp listen(). This protects the parent on every subsequent
close path, including a failed endpoint addition.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm: fix deadlock of mremap() against UFFDIO MOVE

With per-VMA locks, UFFDIO MOVE can run concurrently with mremap()
on different VMAs in the same mm. Those VMAs can share page tables, so
both operations can acquire the same pair of page-table locks.

UFFDIO MOVE orders the locks by address, while mremap() takes the source
lock first. These conflicting orders can deadlock; mremap() holding
mmap lock for writing no longer helps.

Move double pt lock() and double pt unlock() to mm/internal.h and use
them for all page-table moves in mremap(). Preserve the source entry
checks after acquiring both locks. Remove the comments claiming that
exclusive mmap lock makes lock ordering irrelevant.

In move ptes(), make sure to just recheck source and destination PMD
after taking the locks and drop the overly-long comment.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

     move ptes() fixup ]

mm/vma: don't leak the charge for stack growth

acct stack growth() charges stack expansion even without VM ACCOUNT.
This can happen for read-only or MAP NORESERVE mappings created with

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: fail the mount if the casefold flag has changed

An unprivileged user in a user namespace can repeatedly trigger a kernel
warning with their own overlay mounts. They do so by changing the
casefold flag of the topmost layer's empty root, the top directory of
that layer, after the layers are set and before the mount is created.

The casefold flag of a directory makes name lookups in that directory
case-insensitive. All layers of an overlay must agree on casefolding.

ovl mount dir check() reads the casefold flag of a layer root when
fsconfig() sets that layer, and saves the result in ofs->casefold. The
mount is created later, by another fsconfig() call with
FSCONFIG CMD CREATE.

The casefold flag of an empty directory can be changed.

The casefold flag of the overlay root must match ofs->casefold.
ovl get root() copies the flag from the topmost layer root, as it is
when the mount is created. On a mismatch, ovl get root() only does a
WARN ON(), and the mount continues. The check is not a WARN ON ONCE(),
so each such mount warns again.

An unprivileged user needs CONFIG UNICODE, and a tmpfs mounted with the
casefold option in their namespace.

Reproduced by changing the casefold flag of the empty upper directory
after the layers were set and before FSCONFIG CMD CREATE, with tmpfs and
ext4 layers, and as uid 1000 in a user namespace.

Fix this by replacing the WARN ON() with a check that fails the mount
with -EINVAL.

clear node memory tier() calls device unregister() while holding
memory tier lock. A concurrent sysfs read can hold a kernfs active
reference and block in nodelist show() on that mutex. device unregister()
then waits in kernfs drain() for the read to finish and release its active
reference, while the reader waits for the offlining task to release the
mutex.

Return the node's former tier from clear node memory tier(), making the
helper more similar to set node memory tier(), which also returns a
memory tier pointer. Let the caller unlink an empty tier under
memory tier lock before rebuilding demotion targets, then unregister its
device after dropping the lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: fix whiteout creation in casefolded directories

unlink and rmdir fail with EINVAL on an overlay with casefolded
(case-insensitive) layers, if the name exists in a lower layer.
Casefolded layers need CONFIG UNICODE. Root can mount such an overlay,
and so can an unprivileged user in a user namespace, with tmpfs layers.

Overlayfs does not change a lower layer. To remove a name that exists
there, it hides the name with a marker file, a whiteout. It creates the
whiteout in the work directory, a scratch directory on the upper
filesystem, and renames it over the name in the upper directory:

- ovl whiteout() creates the whiteout with mknod, or as a hard link to
 an earlier whiteout.
- ovl cleanup and whiteout() then prepares the rename with
 start renaming two dentries(), which returns -EINVAL if the source or
 the target dentry is unhashed, that is, not in the dentry hash table.

With casefolded directories, both dentries can be unhashed:

- The target. Lookup in a casefolded directory leaves a negative dentry
 unhashed, so the rename target is unhashed if the name does not exist
 in the upper directory.
- The source, which is the new whiteout. tmpfs hashes a dentry when
 mknod or link makes it positive, but ext4 does not, so on ext4 the
 source is unhashed as well.

The cleanup after the failure also refuses an unhashed dentry, so on
ext4 the whiteout is left behind in the work directory.

Reproduced with rm and rmdir on casefolded tmpfs and ext4 layers, also
as uid 1000 in a user namespace.

Fix this by creating the whiteout with ovl create temp(), which repeats
the lookup if the new dentry is unhashed. Prepare the rename with
start renaming dentry(), which looks up the target name with the
directories locked. The caller looked the name up without a lock, so
return -ESTALE if the name now refers to a different inode.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/ksm: check large swap-cache folios before mapping them

KSM folios are always small, but their shared swap slots can be read
back as part of a large folio in the swap cache. ksm might need to copy()
skips large folios, so another process can map a page with an incompatible
anon vma or page index. Reverse mapping then cannot find the new
mapping, preventing migration or reclaim.

Apply the same compatibility checks to large folios as to small ones.
Pass the page corresponding to the swap entry and copy only that page
when necessary. In do swap page()'s copy path, decrement only that slot's
swap count, because the source swap-cache folio can now be large.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

khugepaged: fix readahead lock inversion in collapse file()

collapse file() can call page cache sync readahead() while still holding
source folios locked. If truncate holds mapping->invalidate lock
exclusively and waits for one of those folios, readahead waits for
invalidate lock and neither side can make progress.

We need to release those folio locks before starting readahead. On a page
cache miss, roll back first, populate the collapse range, and retry once.
Doing readahead after rollback avoids an extra pass when all folios are
already present. If another miss occurs on retry, give up rather than keep
retrying while truncate or reclaim removes folios.

Keep page cache sync readahead() and wait for read I/O with
filemap lock folio(), releasing each folio before moving to the next. The
existing uptodate check during collapse still handles read errors.

Shmem uses shmem get folio() for swapin and fallocated folios without
taking mapping->invalidate lock, so it is unaffected.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: Clamp the ATIF backlight curve to its 99 points

amdgpu atif query backlight caps() stores the firmware's number of points
as data points but copies only the 99 points that luminance data[] holds.
number of points is a u8, so a firmware table that claims more makes the
custom curve code in amdgpu dm index past the array, and
dm query extended brightness caps() copy past the end of the
data points[] buffer it fills

Clamp the count to ATIF QBTC MAX DATA POINTS and warn, since a table
that claims more is a firmware bug

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost/vsock: size receive SKBs from declared payload

vhost vsock alloc skb() sizes the skb from iov length(), the total guest
descriptor length. virtio transport inc rx pkt() instead adds hdr->len to
rx bytes and buf used, and budgets each queued skb as SKB TRUESIZE(0). The
guest controls the descriptor length and hdr->len independently.

A guest can therefore provide a 64 KiB descriptor while declaring a zero
payload. The descriptor-sized skb remains queued, rx bytes and buf used
remain unchanged, and only the fixed queue-entry budget limits retention.
This is not a lifetime leak: the skb is freed when dequeued or at socket
teardown. Repeating this across connections can nevertheless exhaust host
memory. On Linux v7.2, 455 such descriptors retained 30,255,680 bytes for
a 262,144-byte receive buffer; a full-payload control retained 265,984
bytes.

Vhost previously read hdr->len and allocated pkt->buf from that value. The
conversion from virtio vsock pkt to sk buff instead allocated receive skbs
from the descriptor length, introducing the allocation-accounting mismatch.

Copy the header into a stack object and validate hdr->len before allocating
the skb. Size the allocation as sizeof(hdr) + payload len so descriptor
capacity no longer determines queued memory. Check payload len against
len - sizeof(hdr) to avoid addition overflow on 32-bit hosts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after defragmenting a bucket

ocfs2 xattr set entry bucket() hands loc.xl entry to ocfs2 xa set() twice:
once for the bucket as it stands, and, if that reports -ENOSPC, once more
after ocfs2 defrag xattr bucket() has packed the name/value pairs down.

Defragmenting ends by sorting the entry array on xe name hash. Buckets
are kept sorted, so the sort only permutes entries that share a hash, but
lib/sort.c is an unstable heapsort and it does permute them. loc.xl entry
is an address inside xh entries[], so afterwards it denotes whichever
entry landed in that slot rather than the one the search found.

The second ocfs2 xa set() then works on the wrong entry. Nothing on that
path compares the entry's name with xi->xi name, so what happens depends
on how the two entries compare in size: ocfs2 xa reuse entry() trips its
BUG ON() when the padded name sizes differ, and otherwise the new value is
written into the neighbouring attribute's value slot while the attribute
being set is left untouched. setxattr() reports success either way.

Remember the entry's hash before defragmenting and look the entry up
again afterwards, the way ocfs2 xattr bucket find() does. An entry that
cannot be found again means the bucket no longer holds what the search
found, so fail with -EFSCORRUPTED rather than writing through the stale
pointer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost add used n in order

vhost add used n in order() advances start by nheads[i] but wraps it
with a single subtraction. If start + nheads[i] >= 2 * vq->num, start
can remain outside the ring.

With used-ring logging enabled, start > vq->num makes (vq->num - start)
underflow. log write() then sets bits beyond the dirty-log bitmap,
potentially corrupting adjacent userspace memory. This is reachable on
the vhost-net TX path with VIRTIO F IN ORDER: done idx can reach
VHOST NET BATCH (64), triggering the issue with a 32-entry ring.

Wrap start with a mask to keep it within the ring. VHOST SET VRING NUM
enforces a nonzero power-of-two ring size, allowing start to be wrapped
using & (vq->num - 1).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved at a fixed address

CMA areas allocated from memblock have their memory accepted by
memblock alloc range nid(), but areas reserved at a fixed address with
memblock reserve() are not.

If a fixed CMA area is requested by the cma=<size>@<base> command line
parameter, it may be in regular RAM and on TDX and SEV-SNP guests it
must be accepted.

Accept the memory of fixed CMA areas as well, so that all CMA areas are
accepted regardless of how they were reserved.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after converting a block to a bucket

ocfs2 xattr create index block() turns a non-indexed xattr block into a
tree by copying it into a bucket, and the copy sorts the entries: a
block holds them in insertion order, a bucket by name hash.
ocfs2 xattr update xattr search() nevertheless relocates the caller's
search by the index the entry had in the block, so unless the two orders
agreed it points at an unrelated entry, and nothing between there and
the write compares that entry's name with the one being set.

Setting an xattr whose new value no longer fits the block arrives here
with xs->not found clear. The block gave up because
ocfs2 xa block can reuse() wants an exact namevalue size match, while
ocfs2 xa bucket can reuse() only wants an entry at least as large as the
new one, so the bucket accepts a pair the block rejected and the update
lands on whichever entry the sort left at that index. Equal padded name
lengths get that other attribute's value replaced in place and its name
left alone, so setxattr returns success while the attribute asked for
keeps its old value. A longer one trips ocfs2 xa reuse entry()'s
BUG ON, and a shorter one is refused by the bucket as well, so
ocfs2 xa prepare entry() wipes the entry and writes the new name over
it, leaving xe name hash describing a name that is no longer there.

Find the entry again by the name being set, matching the type as well.
The copy carries every entry and every name over unchanged, and (type,
name) pairs are unique within a block, so the match is exact. The type
matters because the handlers strip their prefix before calling
ocfs2 xattr set(), so user.foo and trusted.foo share a stored name, a
stored length and a hash, and both can sit in the same block.

The name has to come from xi rather than from xs->here: a failed set can
remove the entry xs->here names, and only the "growing" caller sets
ctxt->set abort, which is what stops the conversion. Scan every entry
rather than narrowing on the hash the way ocfs2 find xe in bucket()
does, since an existing entry keeps the hash it was stored under, which
a kernel that sign-extended the name bytes made different from the one
computed now. An empty result means the entry did not survive the
failed set and this has become an insert; leaving xs->here alone would
keep it pointing into the block, which is rewritten as a tree root
before the caller reads it again.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: grant a POSIX ACL group entry only to the group's members

When no ACE of the DACL matches the caller, Everyone or Authenticated
Users, smb check perm dacl() falls back to the file's POSIX ACL. It
takes the first ACL USER or ACL GROUP entry whose id equals the
caller's uid. For ACL GROUP, this compares a gid with the caller's uid.
A numerical match grants the group's permissions even when the caller
is not a member.

Match a group entry only when the caller is also in the group.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/loongson: Handle buffer mapping failures when clearing a BO

lsdc bo clear() ignores the return value from lsdc bo kmap() and writes
to lbo->kptr unconditionally. When the first mapping of a newly allocated
buffer fails, kptr is still NULL and the subsequent memset accesses it.

Return the mapping error without touching the buffer and propagate it
from lsdc gem object create(). Install the GEM object functions before
clearing so that drm gem object put() can release the buffer correctly
on failure. Do not add the failed object to the tracking list or return
an uncleared buffer to the caller.

Imported buffers still skip clearing, and successfully mapped buffers
are cleared and unmapped as before.

Tested on LS7A2000 with a one-shot range error in ttm bo kmap(). Its
-EINVAL return reached userspace, the object was destroyed once, and
no GEM handle was published. Normal create/map/zero/write/read/close
cycles passed, with the tracked BO count and VRAM usage unchanged.

AI assistance was used for the lifetime analysis, fix, fault-injection
tools, build and test execution.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/shmem: fix accounting of swapin-error markers

A failed swap read replaces the swap entry with a swapin-error marker in
the page-cache and subtracts its pages from "alloced" and "swapped";
however, it leaves their block charge in place.

Removing the marker during truncate then subtracts from "swapped" again.
This can underflow the counters or make swapped reach zero while other
pages remain swapped out, causing swapoff to loop without finding them.

When installing the marker, subtract only from "swapped" and let
shmem recalc inode() reduce "alloced" and release the block charge.

Make shmem free swap() report successful removal separately from the
number of swap pages freed, so removing a swapin-error marker does not
subtract from "swapped" again.

It's a bit confusing, but replacing a swapped out page by a swapin-error
marker in shmem set folio swapin error() behaves as follows:

Initially:
	alloced=1, swapped=1, nrpages=0
Calling shmem recalc inode(inode, 0, -1)
	-> swapped = 0
	-> freed = 1 - 0 - 0 = 1
	-> alloced -= freed
	-> alloced=0, swapped=0, block charge released

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: require DELETE access for delete-on-close opens

smb2 open() accepts FILE DELETE ON CLOSE on an existing file without
DELETE in DesiredAccess. When the request asks only for
FILE READ ATTRIBUTES or READ CONTROL, it also skips inode permission()
and the parent directory MAY WRITE | MAY EXEC check that delete-on-close
is meant to get. The file is then marked for deletion by a caller who
could not delete it.

The unlink happens later, in  ksmbd inode close(), when the last handle
on the inode is closed, and it runs with the credentials of that handle.
If the caller closes last, the unlink fails. If another user who can
write the parent directory, such as the file's owner, still has the file
open, the file is deleted when that user closes it. Until then new opens
of the file fail with STATUS DELETE PENDING. So a user with only search
permission on a directory can delete a file in it, or block opens of it,
while the owner has it open.

A MAXIMUM ALLOWED open that also requests DELETE has the same problem.
The requested access is replaced with the maximal access, which does not
include DELETE when the caller cannot write the parent directory, and the
later permission checks are skipped as already done.

MS-FSA 2.1.5.1 requires an open with FILE DELETE ON CLOSE and without
DELETE in DesiredAccess to fail with STATUS INVALID PARAMETER, and Samba
does the same. Add that check to the CreateOptions validation, using
the generic-mapped DesiredAccess so that GENERIC ALL still qualifies.
This also refuses MAXIMUM ALLOWED with FILE DELETE ON CLOSE but no
explicit DELETE, as MS-FSA and Samba do. When MAXIMUM ALLOWED is
requested with DELETE but the maximal access does not include DELETE,
fail with STATUS ACCESS DENIED. With DELETE requested, delete-on-close
opens go through the existing parent directory check.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/shmem: preserve allocation errors when swapping in large entries

shmem swapin folio() adjusts swap to the requested slot within a large
swap entry before allocating a folio. If allocation or charging fails,
the error path compares this adjusted value with the original entry
still stored in the XArray in shmem confirm swap().

Unless the index is at the start of the entry, this turns -ENOMEM into
-EEXIST even though nothing changed.

The caller retries -EEXIST, so persistent allocation failures can leave
the task spinning instead of returning the error.

Restore swap to index entry on allocation failure so the existing error
path checks the original entry. This preserves the allocation error if
the entry is unchanged and still retries if it changed concurrently.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/mglru: don't use stack pointers when walking PUD and PMD tables

MGLRU passes stack copies of page-table entries in walk pud range() and
walk pmd range() when walking to the next level. These copies can become
stale when khugepaged or MADV DONTNEED (CONFIG PT RECLAIM) removes a PTE
table concurrently.

This pattern dates back to commit bd74fdaea146 ("mm: multi-gen LRU:
support page table walks"). Likely, earlier locking masked the latent
bug. Later changes exposed it: commit 1d65b771bc08 ("mm/khugepaged:
retract page tables() without mmap or vma lock") allowed concurrent
retraction, and commit cf4a65539c13 ("memcg-v1: no need for memcg locking
for MGLRU") dropped the walker's outer RCU protection.

The fix is simple, so just fix the original commit so we don't have to
speculate. To fix it, pass the actual PMD/PUD pointers. This restores the
RCU-protected lookup and validation against the live PMD. Note that the PUD
handling is required as well to handle folded page tables correctly in all
cases.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.
